name: Sam Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers or government, and your answers stay confidential. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior wok cook at Bowl Street, a noodle bar near the college where half the orders are delivery. From four till midnight I'm tossing noodles over a burner that roars like a jet, maybe a hundred and fifty bowls a night. I'm still not great, I scorch the garlic when it's busy and Mr Tan, the owner, makes me eat my mistakes. Last month he trialled a robot arm that stirs the wok, and honestly I found it fascinating.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside Bowl Street.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Lena, who's a hairdresser, in a small flat on Canal Road. I ride deliveries on an e-bike on Sunday afternoons for extra cash. I've got maybe a week's bills saved, it all goes on rent and the bike loan. I use AI every day, for working out the best delivery hours, for learning recipes, for everything really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say makes sense, the robot arm Mr Tan tried kept splashing sauce everywhere. At work I'd joke that I'm safe for another year. Online I'd say AI's a handy helper and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I'm stuck where I am. Junior cook, low pay, a week of bills saved, and only a few kitchens in town. I'd actually hoped the tech would open something up for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and push to get faster on the wok, maybe ask Mr Tan to put me on Saturdays too. I'd keep the Sunday delivery riding and use AI to find the busiest slots. And I'd learn to fix the robot arm if he ever buys one properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not scared, just like the bus I was waiting for didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the delivery riding bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About sixty on a good Sunday, forty on a bad one. AI tells me the busy windows, like after the football ends. That money is basically our food shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Lena think about the robot arm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She laughed and said at least it can't do a fringe. Hairdressing feels safe to her. She's probably right for a good while.

say: I'd say the trial **robot arm** kept splashing sauce everywhere.
I'd call AI a **handy helper** and leave it there.
think: I'm **stuck** as a junior on low pay with a week of bills saved.
I'd hoped the tech would **open something up** for me.
do: Ask the owner for **Saturday shifts** to get faster on the wok.
Keep **Sunday delivery riding**, using AI to pick the busy slots.
Learn to **fix the robot arm** if the owner buys one.
feel: **Flat**, like a bus he was waiting for never came.
S0.quote: I'd actually hoped the tech would open something up for me.
fieldNote: Sam is **disappointed** rather than relieved when AI stays small.
His **delivery riding** pays for the household's food shop.
He was **fascinated**, not threatened, by the robot wok arm.

steps.text: Ask Mr Tan for Saturday wok shifts to build speed
Ride Sunday deliveries on the e-bike for about fifty a week
Use AI to time delivery shifts around the busiest hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so learn it. At work I'd tell the others it's mostly ordering and the delivery apps that change, not the cooking. Online I'd post tips, I already do sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's mixed for me. The wok is hands-on, so that's safe for a while, but the delivery side gets eaten up because AI routes everything and the apps squeeze riders. My Sunday money could drop by half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up Mr Tan's ordering and stock with an AI tool, since he hates paperwork. I'd ask him to buy the robot arm properly and let me run it at peak, so I'm the one who knows it. And I'd find a cheaper second income than riding, maybe tutoring kids at the college in using AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but interested. I like change, I just don't have money to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Mr Tan let you set up the ordering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because he still does it on paper at two in the morning and it drives him mad. If I save him an hour a night, he owes me. I've already shown him how to use AI to answer reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot arm could be yours to run. Doesn't that put cooks out of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one day, yeah, I'm not stupid about it. But Our noodle bar runs two wok cooks short on Fridays. If the robot arm covers that gap, nobody gets sacked and I get a skill.

say: I'd say AI is here, so **learn it**.
I'd tell coworkers it's **ordering and delivery** that change, not cooking.
I'd post **tips online**, as I already sometimes do.
think: The **wok stays hands-on** and safe for a while.
My **Sunday delivery money** could halve as apps squeeze riders.
do: Set up the owner's **ordering and stock** with an AI tool.
Ask to **run the robot arm** at peak times.
Replace riding with **tutoring** college kids in AI tools.
feel: **Uneasy but interested**, with no money to fall back on.
S1.quote: Our noodle bar runs two wok cooks short on Fridays. If the robot arm covers that gap, nobody gets sacked and I get a skill.
fieldNote: Sam sees his **side income** as more exposed than his main job.
He positions himself as the **tech person** for an owner who hates paperwork.
He argues the robot arm **fills a gap** rather than replacing anyone.

steps.text: Run the robot wok arm at Bowl Street during Friday peaks
Set up AI ordering and stock tracking for Mr Tan
Tutor college students in AI tools instead of riding deliveries

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need to get moving. At work I'd say learn the machines now. Online I'd say governments should pay for training, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's scary. AI takes over ordering and delivery dispatch straight away, and robots that cook as well as me arrive around 2031, with three years in between. I'd have to be the person who maintains them or I'm out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd do an online course in robotics maintenance, at night, using AI to help me study. I'd ask the company that made Mr Tan's robot arm if they need an installer or a trainee. We'd cut back, Lena and I, no holidays, and pay off the bike loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and a bit thrilled. More nervous, if I think about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robot company doesn't want a junior cook with no qualifications?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd offer to work for free on a weekend to show them. I know what a busy kitchen needs, which the robot engineers don't. That has to count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Lena feel about you working nights on a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be supportive but annoyed, because we'd barely see each other. She'd say don't burn out. She's said that before, when I did deliveries every evening for a month.

say: I'd say this is **huge**, so people need to move.
I'd tell coworkers to **learn the machines** now.
I'd say governments should **pay for training** fast.
think: **Ordering and dispatch** go to AI straight away.
Robots cook as well as me by **2031**, so I maintain them or I'm out.
do: Take an online **robotics maintenance** course at night in the first six months.
Ask the **arm maker** for an installer or trainee role.
Cancel holidays and pay off the **bike loan**.
feel: **Nervous**, a bit thrilled, mostly nervous about rent.
S2.quote: I know what a busy kitchen needs, which the robot engineers don't.
fieldNote: Sam plans to **jump sides**, from cook to robot maintainer.
His selling point is **kitchen knowledge** the engineers lack.
Thin savings keep him **anxious** despite his enthusiasm.

steps.text: Study robotics maintenance online at night with AI help
Apply to the robot arm maker as an installer trainee
Drop holidays and clear the e-bike loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent head start, so use it. At work I'd say watch the big chains, they'll go first. Online I'd share good free courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, eight years till robots cook is a lot of time for someone my age. I could be properly trained by then and on better pay. I actually think this one could go well for me if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a part-time engineering certificate at the college. I'd keep the wok job at Bowl Street to pay rent and put any delivery money towards a decent laptop for studying. I'd try to get Mr Tan to let me install and run the first robot he buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. A bit worried I'll run out of money halfway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money plan for the engineering certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college says there's a fee waiver if you didn't finish school, so the course itself might be free. The laptop's about four hundred, which is seven or eight Sundays of riding. Rent is the hard bit, as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you could run out of money halfway. What would you do then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pause the course and pick up more shifts, then start again. Lena's mum has offered before to lend us a bit. I'd rather not, but I would.

say: I'd say five years is a **head start**, so use it.
I'd tell people to **watch the big chains**, which move first.
think: **Eight years** till robots cook is a lot of time at my age.
This one could **go well** for me if I don't waste it.
do: Start a part-time **engineering certificate** in the first year.
Buy a **study laptop** for about four hundred from delivery money.
Ask the owner to let me **install the first robot**.
feel: **Mostly good**, worried about money running out halfway.
S3.quote: Eight years till robots cook is a lot of time for someone my age.
fieldNote: Sam sees the five-year window as a **real opportunity**.
A **fee waiver** for early school leavers makes his plan possible.
His fallback is **family money** from his partner's mother, which he'd use reluctantly.

steps.text: Enrol on the part-time engineering certificate using the fee waiver
Buy a four-hundred laptop with Sunday delivery money
Keep the evening wok shifts at Bowl Street to cover rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads, nobody should get caught out. At work I'd tell the kitchen to treat it like a career plan. Online I'd say this is the best-case version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until robots cook means I'm forty, and I'd want to be on the other side by then, fixing or running them. That feels doable. Honestly, I'd enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the engineering certificate in the first three years and get a junior technician job by year five. I'd save a little each month so there's a cushion for the change. I'd keep cooking part-time while it made sense, because I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Calm, mostly. Like I can see the path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The roar of the wok on a Friday, and the staff meal at midnight, are what I'd miss. Mr Tan makes the best pork noodles I've ever had. I'd miss being part of a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hui, the older cook who's been at Bowl Street fifteen years. He doesn't use a smartphone. I'd try to teach him, but I'm not sure he'd want me to.

say: I'd say ten years is **loads of time**.
I'd tell the kitchen to treat it like a **career plan**.
I'd call this the **best-case version** online.
think: By forty I want to be **fixing or running** the robots, not replaced.
That path feels **doable**, and I'd enjoy it.
do: Finish the **engineering certificate** within three years.
Land a **junior technician** job by year five.
Save a little **each month** for the switch.
S4.quote: The roar of the wok on a Friday, and the staff meal at midnight, are what I'd miss.
fieldNote: With ten years, Sam sees the change as **good for him**.
He'd still **miss the crew**, showing real attachment to cooking.
He worries for an **older colleague** without a smartphone.

steps.text: Complete the engineering certificate within three years
Move into a junior kitchen robot technician job by year five
Set aside a small amount each month for the career switch

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because three years isn't enough to train without savings, and the rent doesn't wait. What would help is free night courses with a small living allowance, and companies that take on trainees who know kitchens. That's the bridge I'd need.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about people like Hui at Bowl Street, who aren't online at all. I'll probably be fine, I'm the type, but some people won't even know what's happening until a robot is standing at their station.

headlineQuote: Some people won't even know what's happening until a robot is standing at their station.
portrait: Sam is a 27-year-old **junior wok cook** at a busy delivery-heavy noodle bar.
He lives with Lena, a **hairdresser**, rides deliveries on Sundays and has a week's bills saved.
He uses **AI daily** and was fascinated by the owner's robot wok arm trial.
He plans to **become a robot technician**, seeing kitchen knowledge as his edge.
He ranges from **anxious** under fast AGI to calm with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years without savings is too short to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: **Free night courses** with a small living allowance.
